title: Masters That Decide Everything
subtitle: Items, parties, prices and taxes — the four decisions you cannot undo cheaply
outcomes: Model items with the right type, UOM and valuation method
Configure customers, suppliers and price lists that scale to thousands of rows
Build SST-correct tax templates and know which charge type to use
Import master data without creating decades of cleanup

slides.title: An item is a costing decision wearing a product's name
bullets: Item Type is Stock, Non-Stock, Service or Product Bundle; only Stock items create stock ledger entries
Valuation Method per item: FIFO (default) or Moving Average — mixing methods in one warehouse is how valuations drift
Item variants (template + attributes) or separate items? Variants when stock must be tracked separately by attribute
Item Defaults per company hold the income, expense and stock accounts and the default warehouse
slides.notes: The expensive mistakes are structural: choosing Service for something you later stock, or creating one item per colour when variants would do. Both are fixable, neither is free once invoices and stock exist. Decide valuation method before the first receipt — changing it later requires reposting every ledger entry.

callout.title: Valuation is not a display setting
callout.text: Switching FIFO to Moving Average on live data rewrites every historical valuation. Pick once, in the pilot, and document the choice.

slides.title: Units of measure before anything else
bullets: Every item has a stock UOM; selling and buying UOMs convert into it via UOM Conversion Factor rows
Set 'Must be Whole Number' for pieces, cartons and anything you cannot split
Conversion is multiplicative: 1 Box = 12 Nos means a factor of 12 on the Nos row
The UOM on a transaction drives quantity in the stock ledger but price per chosen UOM
slides.notes: If UOM conversion is wrong, stock is wrong in a way no report flags: quantities look plausible, valuation does not. Test one carton sold in Nos and one sold in Boxes, then check Stock Balance in stock UOM. Malaysian training grant and customs reporting both ask for quantities in specific UOMs, so keep the set small and consistent.

slides.title: Customers and suppliers are ledgers, not address books
bullets: Each party carries a control account, default currency, price list and payment terms — those defaults decide every future transaction
Groups and territories drive reporting and default accounts; two levels of nesting is usually enough
Addresses and contacts are separate DocTypes linked by Dynamic Link — the primary address is what prints and what MyInvois reads
Malaysia TIN, business registration and SST numbers live in custom fields added by the e-Invoice app
slides.notes: A customer record is the default value factory for sales documents: change its price list and every new order changes with it. Keep an address hygiene rule — one primary billing address per party — because e-Invoicing rejects documents with incomplete buyer addresses and because humans read the printed address, not the database.

callout.title: Two identity fields matter
callout.text: LHDN validates TIN plus registration number (BRN/NRIC). Capture both on the Customer, and make the address complete — line 1, city, postcode, state.

slides.title: How ERPNext picks a rate
bullets: Price List on the transaction, then Item Price rows filtered by price list, UOM, customer/supplier, batch and validity dates
Pricing Rules run after the price list and can set, discount, or add margin — by item, group, brand, customer, territory or quantity
Item Price 'buying rate' and 'selling rate' are separate rows; never share one price list across both directions
Selling Price List currency must match the order currency, or the rate is converted at the exchange rate of the day
slides.notes: Rate resolution is layered, and that layering is the feature: one standard price list, then pricing rules for segments, then negotiated item prices for named customers. When a salesperson reports a wrong rate, walk the layers in order rather than editing the line. Also lock down who may edit Pricing Rules — they silently override everything.

slides.title: Tax templates: five charge types, one rule
bullets: On Net Total is what SST needs: rate × net amount, one row per tax account
Actual takes a fixed amount; On Previous Row Amount/Total compound; On Item Quantity is per unit
Tax Category selects the template automatically on transactions (e.g. 'SST Sales – Service 8%')
Item Tax Template narrows exemption per item; 'included in print rate' means the price already contains the tax
slides.notes: Most Malaysian setups need two sales templates (sales tax, service tax) and two purchase templates, plus a zero-rated and an exempt template. The trap is inclusive pricing: if your price list is tax-inclusive, set 'included in print rate' so the ledger posts the right net and tax split. Otherwise the customer pays 8% twice.

slides.title: Warehouses, cost centres and dimensions
bullets: Warehouse is a tree: group warehouses for reporting, leaf warehouses for stock; each leaf can own a stock account
Transit warehouses model goods in motion between sites; use them instead of 'adjustment' entries
Cost Center is mandatory on most expense lines; Project is the second common dimension
Accounting Dimensions add up to five more free dimensions (channel, branch, campaign) reported on every ledger row
slides.notes: Dimensions are cheap to add and expensive to backfill. If the business will ever ask 'profit by branch' or 'cost by channel', create the dimension before the first transaction, because reports cannot reconstruct what was never recorded. Keep the count small: three dimensions is plenty for most mid-sized companies.

callout.title: Name for the report
callout.text: Warehouses and cost centres appear in every report. Name them so a column header is readable: 'Main - PJ', not 'WH01'.

slides.title: Importing master data without regret
bullets: Import in dependency order: UOMs → Item Groups → Items → Customers/Suppliers → Addresses → Price Lists → Item Prices
Use the Data Import tool's template export, keep one row per record, and never import an ID you did not create
Download the error report, fix the sheet, re-import only failed rows — the tool is idempotent per name
Test on a copy of the site; a wrong column in a 10,000-row import is a weekend, not an hour
slides.notes: The classic failure is importing items with a text 'UOM' column that does not exactly match an existing UOM. The import succeeds and creates items referencing nothing. Validate by opening five random imported records and running Stock Balance before declaring victory.

slides.title: Master data review before go-live
bullets: Every stock item has a stock UOM, an item group, a valuation method and per-company default accounts
Every customer and supplier has a control account, currency, payment terms and a primary address
Tax templates exist for every tax situation you actually invoice, and each has been tested on a draft invoice
Price lists are named by purpose and currency; only one is marked default per currency
slides.notes: Run this review as a checklist with sign-off from finance, not as a vibe. In practice the four items above catch ninety percent of go-live defects, and each is a five-minute SQL or report query rather than a project.

callout.title: Prove it with a draft
callout.text: Create one draft Sales Invoice per tax situation. If the tax split and totals look right, your masters are ready.

lab.title: Configure a product, a customer and an SST-correct price
steps: Create UOM 'Box' with a conversion factor of 12 against Nos; mark 'Must be Whole Number' on both
Create Item Group 'Consulting' and Item Group 'Hardware'; add one Service item and one Stock item under them
On the stock item set valuation method FIFO, stock UOM Nos, and per-company defaults for income, expense and stock accounts
Create Customer 'Acme Manufacturing' with MYR, payment terms Net 30, a primary billing address and a Malaysian TIN
Create Sales Tax Template 'SST Sales – Service 8%' with one On Net Total row at 8% against the service tax liability account
Create Price List 'Standard Selling MYR' with an Item Price for the service item; then add a Pricing Rule giving Acme 5% off
Draft a Sales Invoice for Acme with both items, apply the tax category and verify: discount applied, 8% only on the service line, totals reconcile
lab.done: The draft invoice shows the pricing-rule discount, tax on the correct line only, and a grand total you can reproduce on paper.

quiz.question: You need to track the same shirt in five sizes with separate stock. What is the correct model?
options: One item template with a size attribute (variants)
quiz.why: Variants keep separate stock and valuation per attribute combination while sharing one template, pricing and description.

quiz.question: An SST template row uses charge type 'On Previous Row Total'. What have you built?
options: A compounding tax calculated on a previous row's running total
quiz.why: On Previous Row Total compounds; for ordinary SST you want On Net Total.

quiz.question: Prices in your price list already include 8% service tax. Which setting prevents double taxation?
options: Included in Print Rate on the tax row
quiz.why: Marking the tax row 'included in print rate' tells ERPNext the rate already contains tax, so it back-computes net and tax instead of adding on top.

quiz.question: Which is evaluated last when ERPNext resolves a selling rate?
quiz.why: Price list lookup first, then Item Price filtering, then Pricing Rules adjust — except a rate typed manually by the user, which always wins.

quiz.question: What is the safe order for a first master-data import?
options: Items, then UOMs, then Item Groups
UOMs, then Item Groups, then Items, then parties, then prices
Any order — the importer resolves dependencies
quiz.why: Each record links to the previous level. Importing items before UOMs or groups produces records pointing at nothing.

narration: Chapter two is about masters, the four decisions that are cheap before go-live and expensive afterwards. First, items. An item is a costing decision wearing a product name: the item type decides whether stock is tracked, and the valuation method decides how value moves. Choose FIFO or moving average once, in the pilot, and write down why. Units of measure come first, because if conversions are wrong the stock report still looks plausible while valuation drifts. Second, parties. A customer is the default value factory for every future sales document: control account, currency, price list, payment terms. For Malaysia capture TIN and business registration number, and keep one complete primary address, because LHDN validates both. Third, pricing. Rates resolve in layers: price list, then item prices filtered by customer and unit, then pricing rules. When a rate looks wrong, walk the layers instead of editing the line. Fourth, tax. Use On Net Total rows for SST, one row per tax account, and if your prices already include tax, mark the row included in print rate, otherwise the customer pays it twice. Dimensions are the quiet fifth decision: if anyone will ever ask profit by branch, create the accounting dimension before the first transaction. Import in dependency order and test on a copy first.
